questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a System Architect's scope from an Application Architect's scope?
options: The Application Architect focuses on one application's internal design; the System Architect is responsible for how that application fits into and interacts with the broader enterprise landscape
There is no real difference — the two credentials cover identical material
The System Architect only works on security, while the Application Architect handles everything else
The Application Architect works across the whole enterprise, while the System Architect stays inside one org
questions.explain: The lesson frames Application Architecture as staying inside one org's boundary (data model, sharing, one app's performance), while System Architecture starts at that boundary and covers how the org fits into the wider landscape of other systems.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which question is most characteristic of enterprise-level thinking, as opposed to application-level thinking?
options: What's the best object model for this specific process?
Which system should own this data at all, and does Salesforce even need its own copy of it?
What permission set does this one user need in Salesforce?
How do I make this one Flow more performant?
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts application-level questions (object models, Flow performance, one user's permission set) with the enterprise-level question of which system should actually own a piece of data in the first place — a question that looks beyond any single org.

questions.q: According to this lesson, does becoming a System Architect mean an architect no longer needs deep Salesforce platform knowledge?
options: No — the lesson states a System Architect still needs to know Salesforce deeply; what changes is the scope of what they're accountable for, not whether platform depth still matters
Yes — System Architects work entirely outside of Salesforce and never need platform-specific knowledge
Yes — governor limits and sharing architecture become the Application Architect's sole responsibility from this point forward
The lesson takes no position on this question
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly says the enterprise-level questions don't replace application-level architecture skills — a System Architect still needs deep Salesforce knowledge (governor limits, sharing, integration APIs); what expands is the scope of accountability.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in this lesson as a typical neighbor system a System Architect has to account for around Salesforce?
options: A second, unrelated Salesforce Developer Edition org used only for personal practice
An HR/HCM system holding the employee master
A browser extension used by one employee
A personal spreadsheet an individual sales rep keeps on their own laptop
questions.explain: The lesson lists ERP systems, HR/HCM systems, data warehouses, middleware/integration platforms, and legacy systems as the typical categories of systems surrounding Salesforce in an enterprise — an HR/HCM system is explicitly one of them.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the risk of treating 'it works in Salesforce' as the same standard as 'it works for the enterprise'?
options: There is no risk — the two standards are always identical in practice

It risks designing a solution that is correct inside the org's boundary while ignoring how it needs to coexist with the systems around it, which is exactly the gap the System Architect role exists to close
It only matters for companies with more than one Salesforce org
It is a risk only for companies that have never used an ERP system
questions.explain: The lesson's framing is that the System Architect discipline exists precisely because a design can be excellent inside Salesforce's boundary while still failing the enterprise if it ignores how it needs to coexist with ERP, HR, data warehouse, and legacy systems around it.
